title: Idyll 1 and Calverley's translation
short: First of Theocritus' Idylls (third century BC): the shepherd Thyrsis sings the death of Daphnis for a goatherd's prize cup; blank-verse translation by C. S. Calverley (1869).
body: Theocritus, a Greek poet from Syracuse working in the early third century BC (partly at Alexandria and on Kos), invented the literary form later called pastoral. Idyll 1 stood first in the ancient collections and became the model for later pastoral elegy: Virgil's Eclogues 5 and 10, Milton's 'Lycidas', Shelley's 'Adonais' and Arnold's 'Thyrsis' all descend from it. Its structure is a frame dialogue between Thyrsis and an unnamed goatherd, a long description of a carved cup offered as payment, and Thyrsis's song with a refrain. The Greek is in dactylic hexameters in a literary Doric dialect. Charles Stuart Calverley (1831-1884), a Cambridge scholar better known for comic verse, renders it in English blank verse with the refrain kept as a recurring line.

title: Matched compliments and prizes
greek: ἁδύ τι τὸ ψιθύρισμα ... μετὰ Πᾶνα τὸ δεύτερον ἆθλον ἀποισῇ
short: The opening speeches trade compliments of equal length and rank prizes (ram, goat, kid; ewe, lamb): the bucolic world measures art in livestock.
body: Thyrsis praises the goatherd's piping as second only to Pan's, the god of shepherds and inventor of the reed pipe (syrinx); the goatherd answers by comparing Thyrsis's song to falling water and ranking him just below the Muses. Each opens with 'sweet' (Greek hadu), and the sound of the first line (hadu ti to psithurisma, 'something sweet is the whispering') imitates the pine's whisper. The careful matching of speeches is the technique of 'amoebean' exchange used in singing contests (compare Idylls 5 and 8). Calverley keeps the balance but turns the Greek's opening sound-play into the plainer 'Sweet are the whispers'.

title: Pan at noon
greek: οὐ θέμις ... τὸ μεσαμβρινόν ... δριμεῖα χολὰ ποτὶ ῥινὶ κάθηται
short: Piping at noon is forbidden (ou themis) because Pan rests then from hunting and is quick to anger; 'bitter bile sits always at his nostril'.
body: Noon was a dangerous hour in Greek folk belief, when gods and spirits were abroad and Pan, the goat-legged god of Arcadia, slept after the hunt; waking him might bring sudden fear (our word 'panic' derives from his name). Calverley's 'Wrath at his nostrils aye sits sentinel' expands the Greek image of sharp bile (chole) sitting at the nose, a physiological picture of anger (compare Akhilleus's 'bile' in Iliad 18.108-110 and the snorting of an angry animal). The refusal provides the dramatic reason why Thyrsis, not the goatherd, will perform, and fixes the scene's time at the still heat of midday.

title: Daphnis
short: Daphnis is the legendary Sicilian herdsman, the first bucolic singer; versions of his death differ, and Theocritus leaves its cause half-explained.
body: Ancient sources give several stories. Aelian (Varia Historia 10.18) says Stesichorus first made Daphnis a subject of song, and tells how he was blinded after breaking faith with a nymph who loved him; Diodorus (4.84) gives a similar account of the herdsman who invented bucolic song. Theocritus' Daphnis dies 'wasting away' (etaketo) under love, defying Aphrodite, without blindness. Scholars disagree whether Theocritus assumes the nymph story, invents a vow of chastity, or deliberately keeps the cause obscure (see the note on Aphrodite's taunt). Calverley's 'woes' renders algea, 'pains, sufferings'.

title: Priapus and the Fountain-nymphs
greek: τῶ τε Πριήπω καὶ τᾶν Κραναιᾶν
short: The singers sit facing a rustic statue of Priapus, an ithyphallic fertility god, and a shrine of the spring-nymphs: a sacred landscape.
body: Priapus, a god of gardens and flocks whose cult came from Lampsacus on the Hellespont, was represented by roughly carved wooden figures set up in orchards and pastures. Theocritus later makes him one of Daphnis's mocking visitors. The 'Fountain-nymphs' (Greek Kranaiai, 'of the springs'; the reading varies in the manuscripts) are the local water-deities. The elm, oaks and 'Shepherd's seat' complete one of the earliest literary pictures of the pleasant place (locus amoenus) that pastoral would make standard.

title: The carved cup
short: The goatherd's prize is a kissybion, an ivy-wood (or ivy-decorated) cup whose carved scenes Theocritus describes in an ekphrasis modelled on Homer's Shield of Akhilleus.
body: Kissybion is a rustic drinking vessel, probably of ivy-wood, here 'washed with sweet wax' and so new it still smells of the carving-knife. The description (ekphrasis) of its decoration recalls Homer's account of the Shield of Akhilleus (Iliad 18.478-608), but replaces cities, war and law with small pastoral scenes; critics see this as a programmatic statement of Theocritus' art, epic technique applied to humble subjects. Ivy dusted with golden helichryse frames the rim, with a tendril (helix) bearing saffron berries; Calverley's 'woodbine' stands for that tendril. The cup has also been read as a figure for the poem itself: crafted, enclosed, and 'virgin', never yet touched.

title: Three scenes: the woman, the fisherman, the boy
short: A woman between rival suitors, an old fisherman straining at his net, a boy plaiting a cricket-cage while foxes raid: love, labour and absorbed art.
body: The three panels have been read as a progression of human ages (youth in love, old age at work, childhood at play) or of activities (eros, toil, craft). The woman's indifference to her suitors anticipates Daphnis's resistance to love; the fisherman's straining sinews are vivid enough that 'every fibre' seems to fish; the boy, so engrossed in plaiting an akridothera (a trap or cage for crickets or grasshoppers) that he ignores the foxes, is often taken as an image of the poet absorbed in delicate craft. Calverley's 'a miracle of art' renders ti theon daidalma, 'a work of the gods' cunning'. 'Snood' (amphix) is a headband; 'scrip' (pera) is a shepherd's bag.

title: Æolian
short: Greek aiolikon ti thama: either 'an Aeolic marvel' (from Aeolis in Asia Minor) or, more likely, 'a shimmering, intricate marvel' (aiolos, 'quick-moving, varied').
body: The phrase is disputed. The adjective aiolikos can mean 'Aeolian', from Aeolis, the Greek region of north-west Asia Minor (home of Lesbian lyric), which would make the cup an import or a work in the Aeolian style. Many commentators prefer to connect it with aiolos, 'shifting, many-coloured', so that the acanthus border is a 'shimmering wonder'. Calverley's capital and his 'Triumph of Æolian art' choose the geographical sense; Lang's prose instead has 'a miracle of varied work', with a footnote giving 'Aeolian' as the alternative reading. Gow and Hunter both discuss the alternatives. The 'lissom briar' around the cup renders hugros akanthos, 'pliant acanthus', the plant familiar from Corinthian capitals.

title: Calydon
short: The goatherd bought the cup from a ferryman from Calydon in Aetolia, paying a goat and a large cheese: a homely transaction for a precious object.
body: Calydon, in Aetolia on the north side of the Gulf of Corinth, was famous in myth for the Calydonian boar hunt (Iliad 9.529-599). A ferryman from there suggests that the cup has travelled, and the price (a goat and a white cheese) places it within the barter economy of the herdsmen. The detail that the goatherd has never drunk from it ('virgin still') raises its value as a gift and echoes the theme of untouched virginity in Daphnis's story.

title: Hades, 'which brings forgetting'
short: The goatherd's argument for singing: songs cannot be kept in Hades, 'the land of forgetting', so they must be sung now.
body: Greek Hades is the world of the dead, where the shades drink of Lethe ('forgetfulness') in later tradition; Theocritus calls it ton eklelathonta, 'that makes forget'. The line introduces the poem's concern with death and poetic survival, and it anticipates Daphnis' defiant claim that he will be a grief to Love even in Hades. Calverley's 'dim land' gives a shadowy colouring to the plain Greek.

title: The refrain
greek: ἄρχετε βουκολικᾶς, Μοῖσαι φίλαι, ἄρχετ' ἀοιδᾶς
short: The refrain 'Begin, dear Muses, begin the bucolic song' divides Thyrsis's lament into stanzas; it changes to 'begin again' and finally to 'cease'.
body: The Greek refrain (archete boukolikas, Moisai philai, archet' aoidas) addresses the Muses ('sweet Maids' in Calverley). Its repetition gives the song a ritual quality, like a dirge with a choral response. It varies at significant points: from line 94 it becomes 'begin again', and after Daphnis' last appeal to Pan (from line 127) it becomes 'cease, Muses, come cease the bucolic song' (legete), as the song and Daphnis' life end together. Calverley renders this last form 'Forget, sweet Maids, forget your woodland song', which keeps the repetition but changes 'cease' to 'forget', perhaps to echo the 'land where all things are forgot'. Virgil imitated the device in Eclogue 8.

title: Thyrsis of Etna
short: The singer names himself and his home, Mount Etna in Sicily: 'This is Thyrsis from Etna, and this the sweet voice of Thyrsis.'
body: The self-naming acts as a 'seal' (sphragis), authenticating the song as a performer's own. It also locates the poem in Sicily, the land of Daphnis and Theocritus's homeland (he came from Syracuse), and the following stanza maps the island's landmarks against distant mainland Greece. 'Thyrsis' became a stock pastoral name: Virgil uses it in Eclogue 7, Milton in 'L'Allegro' and Matthew Arnold for his elegy on Clough.

title: Where were ye, Nymphs?
greek: πᾷ ποκ' ἄρ' ἦσθ', ὅκα Δάφνις ἐτάκετο, πᾷ ποκα Νύμφαι;
short: The singer asks where the Nymphs were while Daphnis wasted away: in Thessaly (Peneus, Pindus), not in Sicily (Anapus, Etna, Acis). Milton and Virgil imitated the question.
body: The rhetorical question of the absent protectors became a fixture of pastoral elegy. Peneus is the river of Tempe in Thessaly and Pindus the mountain range of northern Greece; Anapus is a river near Syracuse, and Acis a stream below Etna named after the lover of Galatea. Virgil adapted the question for Gallus (Eclogue 10.9-12) and Milton for Edward King ('Where were ye Nymphs when the remorseless deep / Clos'd o'er the head of your lov'd Lycidas?', 'Lycidas' l. 50). The beasts' lament that follows (jackals, wolves, a lion) shows nature mourning, another convention of the genre.

anchor: First from the mountain Hermes came
title: The visitors: Hermes, herdsmen, Priapus
short: A procession of visitors questions the dying Daphnis: Hermes (in some versions his father), the herdsmen, then Priapus. Daphnis answers none of them.
body: Hermes, god of herdsmen and born on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia, comes 'first from the mountain'; ancient tradition sometimes made him Daphnis's father. His question, 'whom do you love so much?', assumes the cause is love. The procession of visitors, ending with the goddess herself, became a convention: Virgil's Gallus is visited by Apollo, Silvanus and Pan (Eclogue 10.19-30), and Milton's Lycidas by Triton, Camus and Saint Peter. Daphnis's silence ('Still naught the herdsman said'), until Aphrodite speaks, is pointed: he will answer only the power he resists. 'He drained ... His bitter portion' renders a repeated verb (anue), 'he was accomplishing his bitter love, accomplishing it to the end of his fate'.

title: herdsman ... goatherd
greek: βούτας μὰν ἐλέγευ, νῦν δ' αἰπόλῳ ἀνδρὶ ἔοικας
short: Priapus mocks Daphnis: called a cowherd (boutas), he behaves like a goatherd, the lowest and most lecherous of herdsmen, watching others enjoy what he will not.
body: Pastoral society in Theocritus has a hierarchy: cowherds (boukoloi) rank above shepherds, who rank above goatherds, and goats are proverbially lustful. Priapus says that as the goatherd watches the she-goats being mounted and pines because he is not a goat himself, so Daphnis watches the girls laughing and pines because he does not dance with them. Calverley tones down the Greek: his kids 'Run riot' and the goatherd 'would frisk as they', where the Greek verb (bateuntai) is frankly sexual. The jibe implies Daphnis is refusing a love that is available, since 'the maid' is searching for him through every spring and grove.

title: Why does Daphnis die?
greek: τὺ θην τὸν Ἔρωτα κατεύχεο, Δάφνι, λυγιξεῖν
short: Aphrodite taunts Daphnis: 'You boasted you would throw Love; has Love not thrown you?' Why he dies is the poem's central crux.
body: The Greek verb lugizein means to bend or throw in wrestling, and kateucheo can mean 'you boasted' or 'you vowed'. So Daphnis seems to have claimed he could defeat Eros. Scholars have argued for three main explanations: Daphnis had vowed chastity and now resists a passion that would break the vow; he loves a girl but refuses to yield to Aphrodite's power; or (following the tradition in Aelian) he is bound by fidelity to a nymph and resists a mortal girl. Gow and Halperin set out the alternatives; Hunter stresses that Theocritus seems to leave the motive deliberately unclear. Calverley's 'try a fall' is the English wrestling idiom, apt for the Greek.

title: Defiance in death
greek: Δάφνις κἠν Ἀίδα κακὸν ἔσσεται ἄλγος Ἔρωτι
short: Daphnis curses Aphrodite and declares that 'even in Hades Daphnis will be a bitter grief to Love'.
body: Daphnis's reply is the poem's moment of heroic defiance. He addresses Aphrodite with three curses ('grievous', 'resentful', 'hateful to mortals'), recognises that his sun has set, and promises to go on harming Eros after death. Critics compare his stance to that of a tragic hero, or to Hippolytus in Euripides, who also refuses Aphrodite and is destroyed by her. Calverley's 'Dead as alive' adds a balance not in the Greek, which simply says 'even in Hades'.

title: Anchises, Adonis, Diomedes
greek: ἕρπε ποτ' Ἴδαν, ἕρπε ποτ' Ἀγχίσην
short: Daphnis taunts Aphrodite with her own humiliations: her affair with the herdsman Anchises on Mount Ida, her love for the hunter Adonis, and her wounding by Diomedes at Troy.
body: Each example turns the goddess's power against her. On Mount Ida near Troy she seduced the cowherd Anchises (the story of the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite); Daphnis, himself a herdsman, tells her to go back to that kind of lover. Adonis, the beautiful youth she loved, was killed while hunting; the Greek says only that he too tends flocks and hunts, a sneer at her taste. Diomedes wounded her in battle (Iliad 5.330-351), so Daphnis invites her to boast to him of beating a mere cowherd. 'Galingale' (kupeiros) is a sedge, and Calverley's 'there are oak-forests; here but galingale' interprets a passage that is textually troubled (l. 105 is marked corrupt, and a line about bees humming at the hives is not printed in every edition).

title: Arethusa and Thybris
greek: χαῖρ' Ἀρέθοισα, καὶ ποταμοί, τοὶ χεῖτε καλὸν κατὰ Θύμβριδος ὕδωρ
short: Daphnis says farewell to the beasts, woods and the Sicilian waters: Arethusa, the famous spring at Syracuse, and the streams of Thybris.
body: Arethusa is the freshwater spring on the island of Ortygia at Syracuse; myth said the nymph Arethusa fled the river-god Alpheus under the sea from Greece to Sicily. Thybris (Calverley's 'Thymbris') was, according to the ancient commentators, a place near Syracuse; its exact identity is uncertain. The farewell to animals and landscape makes Daphnis's death a loss to the whole countryside, and Milton echoes the invocation of Arethusa in 'Lycidas' ('O fountain Arethuse', l. 85).

title: Pan's Arcadian haunts
short: Daphnis calls Pan from his Arcadian mountains, Lycaeus and Maenalus, and from Helice and the tomb of 'Lycaon's son', to come to Sicily.
body: Mount Lycaeus (Calverley's 'Lyceum') and Maenalus are Arcadian mountains sacred to Pan. Where the printed Greek has erion, 'barrow, burial mound', a variant reading is rhion, 'peak'; Calverley takes 'Rhium and Helice' as place-names (Helice was a town of Achaea on the Gulf of Corinth, Rhium a headland on that gulf). Gow, by contrast, takes Helice to be Callisto, whom myth made a bear on the Arcadian mountains, so that the Greek means the high places of Arcadia. The 'tomb of Lycaonides' is identified by Gow with the grave of Arcas, son of Callisto, grandson of Lycaon and eponymous hero of Arcadia (his tomb was shown on Maenalus; Pausanias 8.9.3); Calverley's 'Lycaon's son' translates the Greek patronymic literally. Summoning Pan to take the pipe marks the symbolic end of Daphnis's career as a singer, and after this stanza the refrain changes from 'begin' to 'cease'.

title: The pipe bequeathed to Pan
short: Daphnis gives his syrinx, 'honey-breathing from its compacted wax', back to Pan, its inventor: the bucolic song passes from the dying singer to the god.
body: The syrinx is the Panpipe, a row of reeds bound with wax. Returning it to Pan is both a dedication (worshippers dedicated tools at the end of a career) and a passing-on of the tradition. The line 'For surely I am torn from life by Love' renders 'for I am dragged now by love to Hades'. Calverley's 'arch thy lip' interprets the Greek description of the pipe as 'curved about the lip'.

title: Adynata: the world turned upside down
short: Daphnis calls for nature to reverse itself (thorns bearing violets, deer hunting hounds, owls outsinging nightingales) because 'Daphnis is dying'.
body: This is the classic example of the adynaton, a list of impossibilities used to show that an event overturns the natural order. Virgil imitated it in Eclogue 8.52-56. Calverley alters two items: the Greek has the narcissus flowering on junipers (he writes 'white lilies') and pines bearing pears (ochnas; he writes 'figs'); the pear line (l. 134) is bracketed as doubtful in some modern texts, so editions differ here. The final contrast, owls from the mountains singing against nightingales, inverts the hierarchy of song and leads into the singer's own silence.

title: Daphnis 'went to the stream'
greek: χὡ Δάφνις ἔβα ῥόον. ἔκλυσε δίνα
short: Greek ebe rhoon, 'he went to (or down) the stream': either Daphnis drowned, or (more probably) the phrase is a metaphor for crossing the river of the dead.
body: Aphrodite wished to raise him, but the threads the Fates had spun had run out, and 'Daphnis went to the stream; the eddy closed over the man dear to the Muses, not hated by the Nymphs'. Some ancient and modern readers think he literally drowned (perhaps taken by the nymphs who loved him, as in other myths); others take the stream as Acheron, the river of the underworld, so that 'went to the stream' simply means 'died'. Gow surveys both views. Calverley's 'down the stream' and 'closed the waters o'er a head' favour drowning. Milton's Lycidas, who is drowned, belongs to the same elegiac tradition, and the echo of 'Clos'd o'er the head' is often noticed.

title: The goatherd's blessing: Aegilus, cicada, Hours, Cissaetha
short: The goatherd blesses Thyrsis with honey and Aegilian figs, ranks him above the cicada, hands over the cup, and ends with a comic aside to the goats.
body: Aegilus was a place in Attica noted for figs (so ancient commentators). The cicada (tettix, Calverley's 'cicala') was the Greek emblem of sweet, ceaseless song (Plato, Phaedrus 259b-d). The Hours (Horai), goddesses of the seasons, are imagined washing the cup at their spring, so fresh is its smell. The poem then returns abruptly to the farmyard: Cissaetha ('Ivy', a goat's name) is to be milked, and the frisky she-goats warned lest the he-goat rise against them. The bathos frames the lament within ordinary rural life, and the earthy last line echoes the sexual imagery of Priapus's jibe.
